evidence.note: Published 1925 in the US; copyright held by Loew's Inc. (MGM). The 95-year maximum term under 17 U.S.C. Â§ 304 as extended by the Sonny Bono Copyright Term Extension Act (1998) expired January 1, 2021. Whether or not Loew's renewed in 1952â€“53, the full statutory term has run.

evidence.note: Silent film: the 1925 release carried no synchronized musical score, so the print's images carry no audio copyright. Any accompaniment at original screenings was live and not part of the copyrighted work.

The Photoplay Productions restoration (Kevin Brownlow / David Gill) adds an orchestral score composed by Carl Davis (1987). That score is a separately copyrighted musical work and the recording a separately protected phonogram; neither inherits the print's public-domain status. Released by Warner Home Video, 2005, as part of the four-disc Ben-Hur (1959) anniversary set.

The underlying source is Lew Wallace's novel 'Ben-Hur: A Tale of the Christ' (Harper & Brothers, 1880), which entered the public domain by term expiry long before the film was made. The 1925 screenplay by Bess Meredyth and Carey Wilson is part of the film copyright, which itself expired January 1, 2021.
evidence.source: Duke Center for the Study of the Public Domain, Public Domain Day 2021

evidence.note: The 'Ben-Hur' franchise has supported an MGM remake in 1959 and a Paramount/MGM co-production in 2016, indicating active ongoing commercial use of the title. editorial:
Ben-Hur: A Tale of the Christ (1925) was the most expensive American silent film ever made â€” a production that cost Loew's Inc. (MGM's parent) roughly $4 million after a disastrous start in Rome under director Charles Brabin. Fred Niblo replaced Brabin mid-production, Ramon Novarro took the title role opposite Francis X. Bushman as the treacherous Messala, and the film finally reached American theaters in December 1925. The chariot race was filmed in a purpose-built Circus Maximus replica at Culver City, and early two-strip Technicolor sequences give the climax visual punch that survives in surviving prints. The Library of Congress selected it for the National Film Registry in 1997. The original copyright, held by Loew's Inc., expired January 1, 2021 when the 95-year US term ran out; the photographic print is in the public domain and free to exhibit, stream, edit, or incorporate.

The rights trap is not in the images but in the score. As a silent film, Ben-Hur (1925) has no original synchronized audio â€” the print itself carries no music rights. The most widely distributed version, however, comes from a Photoplay Productions restoration supervised by film historian Kevin Brownlow, with an orchestral score composed by Carl Davis in 1987; Warner Home Video released this restoration in 2005 bundled with the 1959 film. The Carl Davis score is a separately copyrighted musical composition and the recording a separately protected phonogram â€” neither inherits the print's public-domain status. A creator distributing or streaming the Warner restoration with its Carl Davis accompaniment must license that score. Using the raw public-domain print with an original or separately cleared score carries no such encumbrance.
faq: Is the 1925 Ben-Hur print free to use?

The photographic print entered the US public domain on January 1, 2021, when its 95-year copyright term expired. The images are free to exhibit, stream, or edit. What is not free is the Carl Davis orchestral score (composed 1987) on the Photoplay Productions / Warner Home Video restoration: that score is a separately copyrighted work and must be licensed if you use that specific restoration version.
Can I use the chariot race footage commercially without permission?

Yes â€” the footage itself is public domain. Source it from the raw print (e.g., via the Internet Archive) rather than the Warner Home Video restoration if you want to avoid the Carl Davis score copyright entanglement. Verify that the specific copy you use is not a proprietary restoration asserting new rights in the transfer. Also note that the 'Ben-Hur' title may carry active franchise trademark interests tied to the MGM / Warner Bros. Discovery library; consult trademark counsel before naming a commercial product after the film.
